title: Less procedural burden, wider global market access for Indian industry: Defence Export SOP and Open General Export Licence framework simplified to make India a trusted global manufacturing & export partner
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Less procedural burden, wider global market access for Indian industry: Defence Export SOP and Open General Export Licence framework simplified to make India a trusted global manufacturing & export partner
sources.evidenceText:
The Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence has undertaken a comprehensive set of reforms to simplify the Defence Export Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) and the Open General Export Licence (OGEL) framework, in line with Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of making India a reliable, competitive and trusted global defence manufacturing and export partner, while advancing the objectives of Make-in-India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat. Undertaken under the guidance of Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh, these reforms seek to reduce procedural requirements, facilitate faster access to international markets and enable Indian defence companies to respond more effectively to global business opportunities, while ensuring that national security considerations remain fully safeguarded.
DEFENCE EXPORT SOP
Stakeholder consultation has been dispensed with for exports of non-lethal defence items to most destinations, while appropriate safeguards have been retained for sensitive countries.
Stakeholder consultation has been dispensed with for exports of all items for international tenders and exhibitions, enabling Indian companies to showcase their products and pursue international opportunities more expeditiously.
OGEL FRAMEWORK
The OGEL is a standing one-time export authorisation that enables eligible exporters to self-generate export authorisations for multiple consignments of specified defence items, without seeking a separate authorisation for each consignment. It provides greater flexibility while reducing repetitive procedural requirements.
Three existing OGEL SOPs covering major platforms and equipment, parts and components, and intra-company transfer of technology have been consolidated into one unified OGEL SOP, providing exporters with a common and simpler framework.
OGEL validity has been increased from two to three years, reducing the frequency of renewals and associated compliance requirements.
OGEL coverage has been expanded from 41 to all countries, except negative/sensitive nations and those facing UN Security Council sanctions or arms embargoes.
A new provision facilitates Indian companies having long-term contracts or agreements with Foreign Original Equipment Manufacturers (FOEMs). OGEL may be granted for eligible items and the particular FOEM, with validity aligned with the underlying contract or agreement, subject to prescribed conditions.
The range of items covered under OGEL has been expanded, providing greater flexibility to eligible exporters. The revised framework also permits civil-end-use exports of specified parts and components of small-calibre arms and protective equipment, further broadening legitimate international business opportunities.
The reforms move India’s defence export regime towards a more comprehensive and facilitation-based system, reducing routine procedural requirements while retaining appropriate safeguards for sensitive items, technologies and destinations. The measures are expected to particularly benefit Indian defence manufacturers, including MSMEs, by enabling them to respond more quickly to international tenders and exhibitions, access wider global markets and reduce repetitive authorisation requirements. With defence production reaching an all-time high of Rs 1.78 lakh crore and defence exports touching a record figure of Rs 38,424 crore in FY 2025-26, these reforms further strengthen the momentum of India’s defence manufacturing and export ecosystem.

title: Member (IT, Taxpayer Services & Technology), CBIC releases Time Release Study 2026 of Jawaharlal Nehru Custom House
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Member (IT, Taxpayer Services & Technology), CBIC releases Time Release Study 2026 of Jawaharlal Nehru Custom House
sources.evidenceText:
: Mumbai, 28th August 2026
Shri Mohan Kumar Singh, Member (IT, Taxpayer Services & Technology), Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), today released the Time Release Study (TRS) 2026 of Jawaharlal Nehru Custom House (JNCH), during his visit to Mumbai Customs Zone-II. Shri Vimal Kumar Srivastava, Chief Commissioner of Customs, Mumbai Zone-II, senior officers of the Zone and representatives of Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority (JNPA), Port Terminal Operators, Customs Brokers, Trade Associations and other stakeholders were present on the occasion.
Speaking on the occasion, the Member CBIC commended the officers of JNCH and all participating stakeholders for the sustained improvement in cargo clearance timelines, and reiterated CBIC's commitment to using data-driven studies such as TRS to further trade facilitation and Ease of Doing Business. He noted that as India advances towards Viksit Bharat @2047, an efficient, technology-driven and globally competitive cross-border trade ecosystem shall be critical to the nation's deeper integration with global value chains.
TRS is a performance measurement tool recommended by the World Customs Organization (WCO) to assess the time taken for release and clearance of cargo, enabling identification of bottlenecks and targeted trade facilitation measures. JNCH has been conducting TRS annually.
The TRS 2026 report shows that the Average Release Time (ART) for import cargo has improved to 65 hours 53 minutes, down from 72 hours 52 minutes in TRS 2025, a reduction of about 9.6%, despite a 16% rise in the number of Bills of Entry handled. AEO consignments recorded an ART of 40 hours 40 minutes, well within the 48-hour NTFAP benchmark, as against 76 hours 59 minutes for non-AEO consignments.
On the export side, the overall release time for Shipping Bills declined to 195 hours 49 minutes, from 208 hours 15 minutes observed during previous TRS. Further, the customs clearance of exports took only 2 hours 12 minutes on an average, while the remaining time pertained to logistics related operations.
***
Source: Office of the Chief Commissioner of Customs, Mumbai Zone-II / Edgar Coelho/Parshuram Kor

The National Academy of Direct Taxes (NADT), Nagpur, organised the Valediction Ceremony of ‘Uttarayan-2026’, a seven-week Orientation Programme for newly promoted Assistant Commissioners of Income Tax, on August 27, 2026. Hon’ble Justice Anil S. Kilor, Administrative Judge, Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, graced the occasion as the Chief Guest. title: DRI seizes 76 kg methamphetamine tablets in two operations along North-Eastern frontier
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: DRI seizes 76 kg methamphetamine tablets in two operations along North-Eastern frontier
sources.evidenceText:
Continuing its sustained crackdown on narcotics trafficking along North-Eastern frontier, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) in two intelligence-led operations in Assam and Mizoram has seized 76 kg Methamphetamine tablets. Two persons have been arrested under the provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985.
56 kg seized methamphetamine
On 25.08.26, in the latest intelligence led operation, the officers of DRI, assisted by personnel of 38th Battalion, Assam Rifles, Silchar, intercepted a suspect 12-wheeler truck at Lalpani, around 40 km from Silchar near the Assam-Manipur border. The truck was identified from among a large convoy of vehicles arriving from Jiribam, Manipur.
Thorough examination of the truck led to the detection of a specially fabricated concealed cavity in the driver’s cabin behind the driver’s seat, which contained 36 brick-sized packets weighing 1 kg each and 100 smaller packets weighing 200 grams each, containing pinkish-orange tablets suspected to be Methamphetamine.
Preliminary testing of the samples using the field detection kit indicated the presence of Amphetamine. The recovered contraband, weighing 56 kg along with the truck was seized under the relevant provisions of the NDPS Act, 1985. The occupant of the vehicle was also arrested.
Earlier, on 18.08.2026, in another intelligence-led operation along the Aizawl–Champhai Road in Mizoram, officers of DRI intercepted a car at Bung Bangla, approximately 30 km from Aizawl. Detailed rummaging of the vehicle resulted in the recovery of 64 assorted-sized packets containing 20 kg of pinkish-orange tablets suspected to be methamphetamine, concealed inside specially designed deep cavities in the rocker panels/side sills along both sides of the vehicle and in the space between the fuel tank and the floor of the car.
20 kg seized methamphetamine operation
Tests conducted using the NDPS field test kit indicated the presence of amphetamine. Preliminary investigation indicated that the drugs had been smuggled from Myanmar into Mizoram through the Zokhawthar–Champhai sector. The 20 kg contraband along with the vehicle used for its transportation, was seized under the provisions of the NDPS Act, 1985. The driver of the vehicle was arrested.
Methamphetamine is a potent synthetic psychostimulant with a high potential for abuse and dependence. Its illicit consumption can cause serious physical and psychological consequences, including cardiovascular complications, agitation, paranoia and psychosis, while prolonged abuse can lead to severe dependence and neurological and behavioural impairment. Methamphetamine is notified as a psychotropic substance under the NDPS Act, 1985, and its illicit manufacture, possession, transportation and trafficking attract stringent penal consequences.

title: Union Health Ministry Reviews Progress Towards Achieving Malaria Elimination Target by 2030
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Union Health Ministry Reviews Progress Towards Achieving Malaria Elimination Target by 2030
sources.evidenceText:
Emphasising India’s commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goal of malaria elimination by 2030, Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary and Mission Director, National Health Mission (NHM), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, chaired a high-level review meeting with senior officers of the Ministry, National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), Mission Directors of National Health Missions and District Collectors of concerned States and districts.
India has made significant progress in reducing the burden of malaria through sustained and focused public health interventions. Between 2015 and 2025, malaria cases and deaths in the country declined by nearly 80% , while the number of high-burden districts decreased from 155 to 33 . As many as 160 districts reported zero indigenous malaria cases during 2022–2025 , reflecting sustained interruption of local transmission and the success of focused malaria control and elimination interventions.
The review focused on the 33 high-burden districts across nine States and Union Territories, which accounted for 64% of malaria cases and 54% of malaria deaths reported in 2025 . Detailed State-wise reviews were undertaken for Mizoram, Odisha, Tripura, Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Maharashtra.
Smt. Aradhana Patnaik emphasised the need to maintain a high level of vigilance and adopt focused, area-specific strategies to effectively prevent and eliminate malaria. She stressed the importance of effective implementation of District Action Plans in all 33 high-burden districts, along with Village Action Plans in high-burden villages, to ensure targeted interventions based on local epidemiological and geographical conditions.
Highlighting the importance of early detection and complete treatment, the meeting stressed the need to strengthen the Test, Treat and Track strategy. Delays in diagnosis and treatment were identified as critical factors contributing to malaria deaths. States were advised to strengthen active surveillance and ensure uninterrupted availability of diagnostics and anti-malarial drugs, particularly in hard-to-reach and vulnerable areas.
The review also underscored the need to further strengthen surveillance systems and improve data quality. States were advised to review unusually high Annual Blood Examination Rates (ABER) to identify possible duplicate testing, repeated entries and inclusion of asymptomatic screening. It was emphasised that asymptomatic cases detected through mass screening should be reported separately and excluded from API and ABER calculations to ensure accurate assessment of the malaria situation and programme performance.
Smt. Aradhana Patnaik further stressed the importance of intersectoral convergence for achieving malaria elimination. She noted that health interventions alone cannot address several factors contributing to malaria transmission, including water-logging, source reduction and environmental management. States were therefore advised to strengthen coordination with the Departments of Rural Development and Urban Development, as well as Panchayati Raj Institutions, for effective implementation of environmental and vector-control measures.
Greater engagement of Self-Help Groups, community volunteers and Panchayati Raj representatives was also encouraged to strengthen community participation in early reporting of fever cases, identification of water-logging and other mosquito breeding sites, and implementation of source-reduction activities.
The meeting was attended by Shri Prabhakar, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Shri Nikhil Gajraj, Joint Secretary (VBD), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Dr. Tanu Jain, Director, NCVBDC; Mission Directors of NHM; State Programme Officers of the concerned States; District Collectors; Chief Medical Officers and District Malaria Officers of the concerned districts.

title: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) Organises Scientific Conclave on Advancing Quality, Safety and Innovation in Drugs and Phytopharmaceuticals at NIPER Guwahati
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) Organises Scientific Conclave on Advancing Quality, Safety and Innovation in Drugs and Phytopharmaceuticals at NIPER Guwahati
sources.evidenceText:
The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India, organised a Scientific Conclave and Interactive Session on “Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) 2026: Advancing Quality, Safety, and Innovation in Drugs, Food and Phytopharmaceuticals” at the National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPER) Guwahati on 27 th August 2026.
The interactive meeting, organised for the first time in the Northeast region, brought together experts and stakeholders from regulatory authorities, academia and scientific institutions to deliberate on the way forward for strengthening the quality and standardisation of phytopharmaceuticals in the country.
A major highlight of the event was the launch of seven Indian Pharmacopoeia Phytochemical Reference Standards (IPPRS) and five Indian Pharmacopoeia Botanical Reference Standards (IPBRS) by IPC, marking the first-ever introduction of these critical reference standards by the Commission. The standards launched are Andrographolide, Capsaicin, Embelin, Eugenol, Marmelosin/ Imperatorin, Scopoletin, Umbelliferone, Terminalia arjuna, Bacopa monnieri, Tinospora cordifolia, Centella asiatica, Ocimum sanctum.
Phytopharmaceuticals represent an important interface between traditional medicinal knowledge and modern scientific approaches, facilitating the development of safe, effective and standardised plant-based medicines. They have the potential to contribute to drug discovery, affordable healthcare and India's growing contribution to the global pharmaceutical sector.
The launch of the IPPRS and IPBRS marked a significant advancement in the scientific standardisation, quality assurance and regulatory evaluation of plant-derived medicinal products. The reference standards are expected to support the evidence-based development, quality control and therapeutic evaluation of phytopharmaceuticals, thereby strengthening their scientific and regulatory foundation.
The standards were launched by Prof. Ashok Puranik, Executive Director, AIIMS-Guwahati, who also addressed the gathering on the occasion. He described the initiative as a remarkable step towards strengthening the quality, safety and scientific validation of herbal and plant-based medicinal products.
In his inaugural address, Dr. V. Kalaiselvan, Secretary-cum-Scientific Director, Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, highlighted the importance of collaboration with the NIPER Guwahati laboratory in ensuring robust quality standards for phytopharmaceuticals. He emphasised that such collaborative efforts are crucial for advancing scientific standardisation and promoting quality-assured plant-based medicinal products.
The event was also graced by Dr. B. Kumar, DDC(I), CDSCO (EZ), and Dr. Ethengbemo Ezung, ADC, Nagaland, along with experts and stakeholders from the regulatory, academic and scientific communities.
The meeting provided an important platform for interaction among experts from regulatory authorities, NIPER Guwahati and IPC, with a focus on promoting evidence-based medicines derived from medicinal plants. The initiative is expected to strengthen the availability of safe, effective and affordable plant-based therapeutic options while encouraging further research, innovation and scientific advancement in the field of herbal and phytopharmaceutical medicines.

title: DDWS urges States/UTs to facilitate student participation from local academic institutions under JJM 2.0
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: DDWS urges States/UTs to facilitate student participation from local academic institutions under JJM 2.0
sources.evidenceText:
In a significant initiative to strengthen field-based learning and knowledge-sharing, the Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, has urged States/UTs to encourage local colleges, universities and academic institutions to document and publish best practices emerging under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 .
Jal Jeevan Mission has emerged as a significant developmental initiative in the rural drinking water sector, since its commencement and this has led to the emergence of several noteworthy best practices across States/UTs in areas such as community participation, source sustainability, water quality management, operation and maintenance, technology adoption and decentralised governance.
Recognising the value of these field-based innovations, States/UTs have been encouraged to undertake the following:
· Engage local colleges, universities and academic institutions to study and document selected case studies and best practices under JJM 2.0.
· Disseminate findings of these studies through academic journals, institutional reports, newsletters, research papers, websites and other suitable platforms to facilitate evidence-based knowledge-sharing and replication.
· Identify suitable case studies & tour sites and facilitate necessary coordination with local academic Institutions/Schools, District Water and Sanitation Missions (DWSMs) and Gram Panchayats.
· Organise tour for Higher Secondary/Senior Secondary students from nearby schools to Multi Village Schemes (MVS), Water Treatment Plants (WTPs), Intake Wells, modern technologies such as Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) and Internet of Things (IoTs) and National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories ( NABL)-accredited Water Testing Laboratories
The initiative envisages that at least one student tour and one published case study/best practice with local academic institutions shall be undertaken in each district by the end of September 2026 .
Through this initiative, JJM 2.0 seeks to deepen the culture of learning from the field, encourage innovation and make successful rural water supply practices more visible and accessible , thereby contributing to the sustained strengthening of rural water security.

title: “Light is the Most Important Element in Visual Storytelling”: Ravi Varman at NFDC Cinematography Masterclass
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: “Light is the Most Important Element in Visual Storytelling”: Ravi Varman at NFDC Cinematography Masterclass
sources.evidenceText:
:Mumbai, August 28, 2026
On the occasion of World Photography Day, the Department of Masterclasses and Panel Sessions at the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) hosted an inspiring masterclass titled “From Still Frames to Moving Pictures: Ravi Varman’s Journey Through Light” at Audi 2, National Museum of Indian Cinema (NMIC), Mumbai.
The masterclass was conducted by renowned photographer-turned-cinematographer Ravi Varman and witnessed a full house of NFDC officials, filmmakers, media professionals and cinema students. The session offered participants an opportunity to understand the art, technique and creative process behind visual storytelling.
The programme began with a visual tribute showcasing highlights from Mr. Ravi Varman’s distinguished career and some of his iconic cinematic frames. Following the presentation, Shri Rajesh Singla, Director of Finance, NFDC, felicitated the speaker and welcomed the audience. He encouraged the students to make full use of the opportunity to interact with and learn from one of the finest visual artists in the industry.
Speaking about his creative journey, Mr. Ravi Varman shared insights into his approach to photography and cinematography. He explained how art and paintings play an important role in his work, often helping him decide the composition of a frame, colour palette and the visual representation of characters.
Talking about his work on sets, Mr. Varman said that he does not usually prepare detailed storyboards in advance. Instead, he allows his instincts and surroundings to guide him once he reaches the set. He highlighted the importance of light in visual storytelling and said, “Light is the mother of photography and cinematography.”
He also spoke about the importance of understanding a director’s vision. Before working on a film, he studies the director’s story, creative vision and previous work. This helps him develop a visual language that supports the director’s style while also bringing his own unique approach to the project.
The masterclass included an engaging Q&A session, where students asked questions about the technical and creative choices behind several of Mr. Varman’s landmark films, including Barfi! , Goliyon Ki Raasleela Ram-Leela , Sanju , Dasavathaaram and the Ponniyin Selvan series.
Addressing aspiring filmmakers, Mr. Varman encouraged them to give greater importance to art and craftsmanship rather than focusing only on commercial success and box-office numbers. He said, “Commitment to art should stand first; fame will follow.”
The session concluded with a vote of thanks by Shri D. Ramakrishnan, General Manager, NFDC, who appreciated Mr. Ravi Varman’s lifelong dedication and passion for cinematography.
Mr. Ravi Varman is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS), American Society of Cinematographers (ASC), and Indian Society of Cinematographers (ISC). Through his celebrated filmography and commercial work, he continues to inspire young filmmakers and visual storytellers.

sources.evidenceText:
In a shining testament to India's growing emphasis on industry-grade training, the Central Tool Room & Training Centre (CTTC), Bhubaneswar, under Ministry of MSME, has successfully conducted four-week Summer Internship Training Programme during May & June 2026, providing industry-oriented, hands-on training to 8,083 engineering students from 22 States and Union Territories across the country, including 26 international students from Sudan and Yemen.
The Training Programme provided an opportunity for engineering students from first year to final year and witnessed participation from across the country, including international students. The programme stands as a proud reaffirmation of CTTC Bhubaneswar's role as a premier institution for offering structured and industry-oriented training designed to sharpen the employability and technical competence of India's youth.
A Spectrum of Opportunity
Spanning disciplines as varied as Mechanical, Electrical, Electronics, Civil, and Computer Science, the programme also focused on emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI - ML), Cloud Computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and Additive Manufacturing. Each four-week course was designed to provide intensive hands-on training, bridging the gap between classroom learning and industrial practice.
Of the 8,083 students trained, the Mechanical discipline led the way with 3,193 candidates, followed by Electronics with 2,209; IT & Software with 1,948; Civil with 388, and other emerging domains accounting for 345- a spread that reflects both the enduring strength of core engineering and the rising pull of new-age technologies. The programme offered training across 39 engineering and emerging technology domains, with the highest participation in Artificial Intelligence (1,748 students), PLC Programming (1,000), AutoCAD (991), Python Programming (413) and Data Analytics (392).
The internship also attracted students from premier institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), National Institutes of Technology (NITs), various Deemed-to-be Universities, engineering colleges, and polytechnic institutes.
About CTTC, Bhubaneswar-
Central Tool Room & Training Centre, Bhubaneswar has been set up to fulfill the tooling and training needs of the Micro, Small & Medium enterprises in the field of Tool Design and Manufacture and training of technical personnel in these fields.
The Centre Offers various services in the area of Auto parts, high precision parts, General Engineering sector by designing, development and manufacturing of quality press tools, moulds & dies, gauges, jigs & fixtures, etc. It also provides training/programmes in Tool & Die technology, Product Design, Mechatronics, Advance Machine Maintenance, CAD/CAM/CAE, CNC machining and programming, etc.
It has manufactured & supplied 437 types of 54,000 precision components to India Space Research Organization (ISRO) for Chandrayaan-3 Mission launched on 14 th July, 2023.
It has also manufactured & supplied different types of precision components like regulator, flow control valves, gyroscope, temperature sensor & navigation parts to ISRO for Aditya – L1 Mission (Indian Solar Mission) launched on 02 nd September, 2023.
The Centre has also made significant contributions to the aerospace and defence sectors by manufacturing high-precision components for Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), including components for the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) programme, thereby supporting indigenous manufacturing capabilities.

title: NTPC WR-I HQ Organises Regional Joint Productivity Council Meeting at Mahabaleshwar
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: NTPC WR-I HQ Organises Regional Joint Productivity Council Meeting at Mahabaleshwar
sources.evidenceText:
Mumbai, August 25, 2026
NTPC Western Region-I Headquarters, Mumbai, organised the Regional Joint Productivity Council (RJPC) Meeting 2026 at Mahabaleshwar on August 25, 2026, bringing together the management and representatives of Unions and Associations from across the Western Region-I.
The meeting was graced by Shri E. Satya Phani Kumar, Regional Executive Director (West-I), along with the Business Unit Heads of NTPC WR-I Projects/Stations at Mouda, Solapur, Anta, Jhanor-Gandhar and Kawas. Ms. Vandana Chaturvedi, Regional Head of HR (West-I), was also present, along with the Heads of HR of WR-I Projects/Stations at Mouda, Solapur, Anta, Jhanor-Gandhar, Kawas and RGPPL.
The meeting also witnessed the participation of representatives of various Unions and Associations from NTPC WR-I Projects/Stations. The Executive Director (DRC), along with the members of the Departmental Review Committee (DRC), was also present on the occasion.
A key highlight of the meeting was the presentations given by the representatives of the Unions and Associations on contemporary and significant themes relevant to the power sector. The discussions focused on:
Flexibilization in Thermal Projects: Quick Response to Changing Grid Demand
Strengthening Safety Culture through Behavioural Interventions
Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing the Efficiency of Power Plants
Zero Demurrage in Coal-Based Plants and Future Sustainability of Gas-Based Plants
The deliberations provided a constructive platform for meaningful dialogue, exchange of ideas and collaborative discussions between the management and employee representatives, with a focus on enhancing productivity, operational excellence, safety and sustainability.
Speaking on the occasion, Shri E. Satya Phani Kumar, Regional Executive Director (West-I), said, “The RJPC is an important platform for strengthening mutual trust and fostering a culture of partnership between management and employees. The ideas and suggestions shared during such forums are valuable in driving productivity, innovation and organisational excellence. As the power sector undergoes rapid transformation, our collective strength lies in working together with a shared vision to meet future challenges and contribute towards building a sustainable and efficient energy future.”
Ms Vandana Chaturvedi, Regional Head of HR (West-I), said, “The active participation of our Unions and Associations reflects the spirit of constructive engagement that is deeply embedded in NTPC’s work culture. RJPC provides an opportunity to collectively deliberate on issues that impact our people and business, while reinforcing the importance of safety, innovation, technology and employee participation.”
On August 26, 2026, a special awareness session on Nuclear Power was also organised for the participants. The session was taken by Shri Nirbhay Gupta, Executive Director (Nuclear), and Shri A. P. Samal, Executive Director (Nuclear), who highlighted the prospects of nuclear power and created awareness about nuclear power plants and their role in India’s evolving energy landscape. The session provided valuable insights into the importance and potential of nuclear energy as a key component of the country’s future energy mix.
The meeting concluded with a shared commitment to strengthen constructive industrial relations and employee participation further, while collectively contributing to NTPC’s continued journey of excellence and leadership in the evolving energy landscape.
***
Neha Kulkarni/Parshuram Kor

title: PARIVARTAN Scheme gains momentum: 1,300+ beneficiaries registered, 42 Banks/NBFCs and 15 auto OEMs onboarded across Delhi-NCR
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: PARIVARTAN Scheme gains momentum: 1,300+ beneficiaries registered, 42 Banks/NBFCs and 15 auto OEMs onboarded across Delhi-NCR
sources.evidenceText:
The Union Cabinet, on 3 rd June 2026, approved the PARIVARTAN (Programme for Accelerated Renewal and Incentivization of Vehicle Assets for Reducing Transport Air Pollution and Network Emissions) Scheme, to replace over 2 lakh trucks and buses conforming to Bharat Stage (BS)-IV or prior emission norms, registered in the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the NCR districts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, with BS-VI or stricter norm compliant or electric vehicles. The Scheme is being funded through the National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB) under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) and is being implemented by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH).
The Scheme has a total financial outlay of ₹9,585 crore, including ₹5,041 crore in budgetary support from the Central Government. Eligible beneficiaries purchasing new BS-VI or stricter norm compliant diesel or CNG vehicles, or electric vehicles, are entitled to a package of incentives comprising:
5% interest savings on eligible vehicle loans for 5 years;
100% Road Tax Waiver for a period of 10 years and a full waiver on registration fees (the States of Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have already issued notifications in this regard);
at least 8% discount on ex-showroom price from participating Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs); and
monthly fuel vouchers ranging from ₹1,200 to ₹4,800, depending on vehicle category, for a period of five years for buyers of BS-VI diesel or CNG vehicles, or a one-time incentive ranging from ₹64,000 to ₹2.56 lakh for buyers of electric vehicles.
The Scheme was launched on 14 th July 2026 . As on 27 th Aug 2026, 1,300+ beneficiaries have registered on the PARIVARTAN Portal. To extend financing support, 42 banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) have been onboarded to provide interest subvention on vehicle loans. On the industry side, Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) have been signed with 15 auto OEMs to extend the discount to eligible beneficiaries.
A multi-pronged awareness campaign is being undertaken to reach eligible vehicle owners across Delhi-NCR regarding the benefits and registration process under the Scheme. The campaign spans print, electronic and digital media, and outdoor publicity at fuel stations, transport nagars, toll plazas and Regional Transport Offices (RTOs) across Delhi-NCR, with the aim of driving wider beneficiary registration and participation under the Scheme.
Sh. Mahendra Singh becomes the first vehicle owner to purchase a new vehicle under the PARIVARTAN Scheme, in Alwar, Rajasthan on 19 th August 2026.
***
GDH/DS/HJ

title: From Private Driver to Self-Employed Autorickshaw Owner: How NBCFDC Support Transformed Sunil Kumar K.P.’s Livelihood
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: From Private Driver to Self-Employed Autorickshaw Owner: How NBCFDC Support Transformed Sunil Kumar K.P.’s Livelihood
sources.evidenceText:
Sunil Kumar K.P., a member of the OBC Thiyya community in Kerala, transformed his livelihood from low-paid private driving to self-employment as an autorickshaw owner with assistance under the National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC) Scheme.
Before receiving assistance, Sunil worked as a private vehicle driver and earned only ₹5,000 per month. Although he possessed driving experience, his limited income prevented him from purchasing a vehicle of his own and improving his livelihood.
His primary barrier was economic. His modest earnings were insufficient to meet household expenses and save enough to invest in a vehicle, keeping him dependent on private driving work.
Despite these difficulties, Sunil aspired to own a vehicle, use his driving skills to become self-employed and achieve greater financial stability for his family.
A turning point came in 2022 when Sunil learned about the NBCFDC loan scheme through the Kerala State Backward Classes Development Corporation (KSBCDC) and received a term loan of ₹2.69 lakh.
Sunil utilised the assistance to purchase an autorickshaw and began working as a self-employed driver, enabling him to benefit directly from his efforts and experience.
The scheme intervention brought a substantial improvement in his earnings. His monthly income increased fourfold, from ₹5,000 before receiving the loan to approximately ₹20,000 after starting his autorickshaw enterprise.
The enhanced income strengthened his family’s financial security, made it easier to meet household expenses and improved their quality of life.
Sunil expressed his gratitude for the support and said,
“The term loan of ₹2.69 lakh helped me purchase my own autorickshaw and become self-employed. My monthly income increased from ₹5,000 to approximately ₹20,000, bringing greater financial stability and a better quality of life to my family.”
Sunil’s journey demonstrates how timely access to affordable credit can help skilled individuals overcome economic barriers, acquire livelihood assets and achieve sustainable self-employment.
*****

title: From Financial Struggle to Mechanised Sanitation Entrepreneurship: How NAMASTE–SUY Support Strengthened Kapil Pal’s Livelihood
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: From Financial Struggle to Mechanised Sanitation Entrepreneurship: How NAMASTE–SUY Support Strengthened Kapil Pal’s Livelihood
sources.evidenceText:
For sanitation workers supporting large families, limited financial resources and the absence of mechanised equipment can make it difficult to build a stable livelihood. Structured financial assistance can help them expand their work, improve their earnings and serve their communities with greater safety and dignity.
Demonstrating the impact of support under the Swachhta Udyami Yojana (SUY) component of the NAMASTE Scheme, Kapil Pal, a 32-year-old sanitation worker from Noor Nagar, Sihani, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, strengthened his livelihood through mechanised sewer and septic tank sanitation services.
Belonging to the OBC/Gadaria community, Kapil completed his education up to the 12th standard and entered sanitation-related work to support his family. He lives in a joint family with his wife, two children, parents and elder brother. His wife is a homemaker, while his elder brother’s contribution to the household income is limited. As the primary earning member, Kapil bears most of the responsibility for meeting household expenses and supporting the needs of the entire family.
Kapil has a four-year-old son and a seven-year-old daughter, who is studying in the second standard. He aspired to improve his family’s financial condition, provide quality education to his children and build a secure future through self-employment.
Before receiving assistance, Kapil faced limited financial resources, heavy family responsibilities and dependence on sanitation work for regular income. The lack of capital and limited opportunities for livelihood expansion made it difficult for him to achieve long-term financial security.
A major challenge emerged when Kapil had to undergo a back operation. The treatment created physical, emotional and financial stress, as unexpected medical expenses added to his existing household responsibilities.
Kapil received assistance under the Swachhta Udyami Yojana component of the NAMASTE Scheme on 21 September 2021. He was provided upfront capital subsidy for the procurement of a tractor-cum-suction machine to strengthen his sanitation service-related livelihood activities.
The project involved a total cost of ₹8.90 lakh, comprising a loan of ₹5,42,500 and a capital subsidy of ₹3,47,500. Kapil is repaying the loan through a monthly instalment of ₹18,640, with approximately ₹1,21,000 currently remaining outstanding.
The mechanised equipment enabled Kapil to strengthen and expand his work through suction-machine operations under Nagar Nigam Ghaziabad. He now provides sewer and septic tank sanitation services primarily in the Raj Nagar Extension area.
Following the intervention, Kapil’s livelihood and economic condition improved significantly. He now earns approximately ₹35,000–₹40,000 per month, enabling him to meet household responsibilities, support his children’s education and build savings for unforeseen circumstances.
The benefits of his improved financial position became especially evident during his recent back operation. Kapil was able to meet the entire cost of his medical treatment independently through savings generated from his sanitation service work, without creating additional financial pressure on his family.
The assistance has strengthened Kapil’s confidence, financial independence and social dignity. He is now better equipped to support his family, fulfil his responsibilities and face future challenges with greater security.
Expressing his satisfaction with the support received under the Scheme, Kapil Pal said,
“The support helped me strengthen my sanitation service work and improve my income. I now earn approximately ₹35,000–₹40,000 per month. The savings from my work enabled me to meet the expenses of my back operation independently while continuing to support my family and my children’s education.”
Kapil Pal’s journey demonstrates how structured financial assistance, mechanisation and livelihood support can empower sanitation workers to become self-reliant entrepreneurs. The intervention under NAMASTE–SUY reflects the Government’s commitment to promoting safe sanitation practices, sustainable livelihoods and dignified economic opportunities for sanitation workers.
Today, Kapil stands as an inspiring example of resilience and self-reliance—serving his community while building a more secure and dignified future for his family.
*****

title: From Financial Challenges to an Academic Career: How NFSC Support Empowered Dr Janaki Sundararajan
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: From Financial Challenges to an Academic Career: How NFSC Support Empowered Dr Janaki Sundararajan
sources.evidenceText:
For full-time research scholars from modest families, meeting the cost of advanced education can be difficult. Timely fellowship assistance can reduce this burden and allow scholars to pursue their academic ambitions with greater confidence and focus.
Demonstrating the impact of support under the National Fellowship for Scheduled Caste Students (NFSC) Scheme, Dr Janaki Sundararajan, a 32-year-old scholar from Dindigul, Tamil Nadu, overcame financial and academic barriers to complete her Ph.D. and build a career in teaching and research.
Before receiving assistance under the NFSC Scheme, Dr Janaki faced financial difficulties in managing research expenses and academic activities during her Ph.D. period from 2019 to 2024. As a full-time research scholar, balancing personal responsibilities and continuing her research without stable financial support was challenging.
She also experienced difficulty in accessing research materials and digital resources, attending conferences, conducting fieldwork, collecting data, travelling for academic purposes and undertaking publication-related activities. Limited financial support affected her ability to focus completely on her doctoral research.
Despite these constraints, Dr Janaki remained committed to her academic journey. She aspired to complete her Ph.D. and become a dedicated academician and researcher in the field of education, with a focus on teacher education, digital education and quality research in higher education institutions.
Dr Janaki comes from a modest family background where education was considered important despite financial limitations. Her family continuously encouraged her higher education journey, but meeting the expenses associated with full-time research placed considerable pressure on the household.
She began receiving assistance under the NFSC Scheme in September 2019. Under the Scheme, she received a Senior Research Fellowship of ₹35,000 per month.
The fellowship helped her manage expenses related to research materials, internet access, data collection, academic travel and publication activities. It reduced financial stress and enabled her to focus more effectively on completing her Ph.D. with confidence and dedication.
Beyond financial assistance, the NFSC fellowship provided Dr Janaki with stability and motivation throughout her doctoral journey. It supported her academic activities, research work and professional development while reducing the financial burden on her family.
With the support received under the NFSC Scheme, she gained the confidence to continue her Ph.D. research without interruption and devote greater attention to academic activities, research publications and professional development. The assistance strengthened both her professional growth and personal confidence.
Dr Janaki is currently working as a Guest Teacher at The Gandhigram Rural Institute (Deemed to be University). The fellowship has strengthened her academic career path and enabled her to move closer to her goal of contributing to education through teaching and research.
Dr Janaki expressed her gratitude for the fellowship support and said,
“The NFSC fellowship provided me with financial stability and the confidence to continue my Ph.D. research without interruption. It reduced the financial burden on my family, supported my research and professional development, and strengthened my path towards a career in teaching and research.”
Through determination and support under the NFSC Scheme, Dr Janaki progressed from facing financial challenges during full-time research to completing her Ph.D. and pursuing an academic career. Her journey reflects the important role of fellowship assistance in advancing research aspirations and strengthening professional opportunities.
*****
SS-53-TAR-KV-GA-RK

title: Government Strengthens Monitoring and Timely Delivery of Scheduled Caste Welfare Schemes
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Government Strengthens Monitoring and Timely Delivery of Scheduled Caste Welfare Schemes
sources.evidenceText:
The Government is implementing a comprehensive range of welfare schemes for the educational advancement, socio-economic empowerment, livelihood promotion and protection of Scheduled Caste communities across the country.
During the financial years 2021-22 to 2025-26, funds were allocated for major initiatives including the Post-Matric Scholarship for SC Students, National Fellowship for SC Students, National Overseas Scholarship, Top Class Education, Free Coaching, Pre-Matric Scholarship, Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojana (PM-AJAY), Scheme of Residential Education for Students in High Schools in Targeted Areas (SHRESHTA), Venture Capital Fund for SCs and skill-development programmes.
The implementation and utilisation of funds under various Scheduled Caste welfare schemes are undertaken in coordination with the respective States and Union Territories. Release of funds is linked to the receipt of complete proposals, submission of Utilisation Certificates, onboarding onto SNA-SPARSH wherever applicable, adherence to scheme guidelines and compliance with the prescribed financial norms.
To improve expenditure and strengthen accountability, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment conducts regular internal reviews of the schemes. Third-party evaluations and social audits are also undertaken to assess implementation and enhance the effectiveness of programme delivery.
Scholarship assistance is largely disbursed through the Direct Benefit Transfer mode to facilitate faster and more transparent transfer of benefits directly into the bank accounts of eligible students. This mechanism also supports accurate beneficiary targeting and reduces delays in disbursement.
The Ministry regularly monitors scheme implementation through national-level Chintan Shivirs, regional meetings, national conferences and consultations with stakeholders and officials from States and Union Territories.
Monthly and quarterly expenditure targets are reviewed to identify implementation gaps and facilitate timely corrective measures. Awareness and outreach initiatives are also undertaken through advertisements in national and regional newspapers, social media campaigns and regular follow-up with States and Union Territories.
These efforts are aimed at increasing awareness among eligible beneficiaries, improving the submission of proposals and ensuring timely utilisation of allocated funds.
Through strengthened monitoring, digital fund-management systems, direct transfer of benefits, regular evaluation and closer coordination with implementing authorities, the Government remains committed to ensuring that Scheduled Caste welfare schemes reach eligible beneficiaries effectively.
The initiatives seek to advance education, dignity, livelihood security and socio-economic empowerment among Scheduled Caste communities across the country.
********
PR-89 TAR/KV/GA/RK

title: India's Index of industrial production records growth of 6.7% in July 2026
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: India's Index of industrial production records growth of 6.7% in July 2026
sources.evidenceText:
In July 2026, Index of Industrial Production recorded a 6.7% year-on-year growth, supported by 7.3% growth in Manufacturing sector and strong growth of 8.7% in Electricity & Gas Supply sector.
The Quick Estimate of Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is released on 28 th of every month (or next working day if 28 th is a holiday). The index is compiled with data received from source agencies, which in turn receive the data from the producing factories/ establishments. These Quick Estimates will undergo revision in subsequent releases as per the revision policy of IIP.
2. Key Highlights:
The IIP growth rate for the month of July 2026 is 6.7 percent which was 7.3 percent (Quick Estimate) in the month of June 2026.
The growth rates of the sectors, Mining & Quarrying, Manufacturing, Electricity & Gas Supply and Water Supply, Sewerage & Waste Management for the month of July 2026 are (-) 0.9 percent, 7.3 percent, 8.7 percent and 7.4 percent respectively.
The Quick Estimate of IIP stands at 124.8 against 117.0 in July 2025. The indices of Industrial Production for Mining & Quarrying, Manufacturing, Electricity & Gas Supply and Water Supply, Sewerage & Waste Management for the month of July 2026 stand at 94.4, 127.4, 133.5 and 148.4 respectively.
Within the Manufacturing sector, 19 out of 23 industry groups at NIC 2 digit-level have recorded a positive growth in July 2026 over July 2025. The top three positive contributors for the month of July 2026 are – “Manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers” (22.2%), “Manufacture of electrical equipment” (28.3%), and “Manufacture of machinery and equipment n.e.c.” (12.1%).
In the industry group “Manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers” item groups “Auto Components, Spares and Accessories”, “Passenger Cars”, and “Commercial Vehicles” have shown significant contribution in growth.
In the industry group “Manufacture of electrical equipment”, item groups “Electrical Apparatus for Switching or Protecting Electrical Circuits (e.g., Switchgear, Circuit Breakers/Switches, Control/Meter Panels) and Parts Thereof”, “UPS and Solid-State Drives”, and “End-Face Connectors for Optical Fibres and Cables” have shown significant contribution in growth.
In the industry group “Manufacture of machinery and equipment n.e.c.”, item groups “Construction Machinery/Equipment (Incl. Bulldozers and Road Rollers)”, “Pumps of All Types (Centrifugal, Hydraulic, Positive Displacement, Gear, Screw, Gravity, Steam, Boiler Feed, Valveless Pumps, etc.)”, and “Steam/Vapour, Wind and Other Turbines” have shown significant contribution in growth.
As per the Use-Based Classification, the indices stand at 115.9 for Primary Goods, 141.8 for Capital Goods, 130.9 for Intermediate Goods and 136.2 for Infrastructure/ Construction Goods for the month of July 2026. Further, the indices for Consumer durables and Consumer non-durables stand at 129.9 and 113.7 respectively.
The corresponding growth rates of IIP as per Use-Based Classification in July 2026 over July 2025 are 4.1 percent in Primary Goods, 16.1 percent in Capital Goods, 10.0 percent in Intermediate Goods, 6.9 percent in Infrastructure/ Construction Goods, 10.5 percent in Consumer durables and (-)1.0 percent in Consumer non-durables (Statement III). Based on Use-Based Classification, top three positive contributors to the growth of IIP for the month of July 2026 are Intermediate Goods, Capital Goods and Primary goods.
Along with the Quick Estimate of IIP for the month of July 2026, the indices for June 2026 have undergone final revision in the light of the updated data received from the source agencies.
The Quick Estimates for July 2026 and the final revision for June 2026 have been compiled at weighted response rates of 88.9 percent and 93.0 percent respectively.
Details of Quick Estimates of the Index of Industrial Production for the month of July 2026 at Sector, Sub-Sector, 2-digit level of National Industrial Classification (NIC-2025), by Use-Based Classification and are given at Statements I, II (A, B, C, D) and III respectively. Also, for users to appreciate the changes in the industrial sector, Statement IV provides month-wise indices for the last 13 months, by industry groups (as per 2-digit level of NIC-2025), sectors and Sub-Sectors.
Release of the IIP for August 2026 will be on Monday, 28th September 2026.
Note: -
This Press Release (English and Hindi Version) is also available at the Ministry’s Website - http://www.mospi.gov.in .
Detailed data pertaining to IIP is available at https://esankhyiki.mospi.gov.in/macroindicators?product=iip

title: From Financial Inclusion to Economic Empowerment: Union Minister Smt. Annpurna Devi Hails 12 Years of the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: From Financial Inclusion to Economic Empowerment: Union Minister Smt. Annpurna Devi Hails 12 Years of the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana
sources.evidenceText:
Union Minister of Women and Child Development, Smt. Annpurna Devi has hailed the completion of 12 years of the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana, describing its journey as one from financial inclusion to economic empowerment.
In a post on 'X' the Union Minister said that under the visionary leadership of the Hon’ble Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi, the Jan-Dhan Yojana has connected crores of citizens – especially women and rural families – with the formal banking system, and built a strong foundation of financial self-reliance.
Sharing the achievements of the scheme, she said that more than 59 crore Jan-Dhan accounts have been opened, of which 56% belong to women and 78% are in villages and small towns. Deposits in these accounts have crossed Rs. 3.1 lakh crore, and Rs. 53 lakh crore has been transferred directly to beneficiaries through the JAM (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile) trinity.
The Union Minister said that this is not merely a scheme for opening bank accounts, but a transformative journey of dignity, security and empowerment.

title: Prime Minister Narendra Modi interacts with youth virtually at IIT Bombay through Khelo India Dialogue; students reaffirm commitment to a drug-free India
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Prime Minister Narendra Modi interacts with youth virtually at IIT Bombay through Khelo India Dialogue; students reaffirm commitment to a drug-free India
sources.evidenceText:
: Mumbai, 28 August 2026
On the occasion of National Sports Day, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi interacted virtually with the youth of the country on 27 August 2026 through the Khelo India Dialogue.
In Mumbai, the Khelo India Dialogue was organised by IIT Bombay at its campus in coordination with My Bharat Mumbai. A large number of students and young participants attended the live virtual interaction and actively participated in the programme. The programme was attended by Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri Ramdas Athawale, International Heptathlon Athlete Ms. Nandini Agasara, Director, IIT Bombay, Prof. Shireesh Kedare, My Bharat Maharashtra State Director Shri Amit Punde, and Deputy Director, My Bharat Mumbai, Shri Anup Ingole.
During the virtual Khelo India Dialogue, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi highlighted the importance of sports in daily life and encouraged the youth to make sports and physical activity an integral part of their lifestyle. PM Modi also spoke about his vision for strengthening India’s sporting ecosystem and the country’s aspirations for the 2036 Olympic Games. He emphasised the need to develop a strong sporting culture across the country and encouraged greater participation of young people in sports. The interaction provided an opportunity for the youth to connect directly with the Prime Minister and understand the Government’s vision for making India a stronger sporting nation.
Addressing the gathering, Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri Ramdas Athawale also emphasised the importance of creating a Nasha-Mukta IIT Bombay and urged the youth to stay away from drugs and substance abuse. He highlighted the importance of a healthy, disciplined and productive lifestyle for the overall development of young people and called upon students to become ambassadors of a drug-free society.
An engaging question-and-answer session was also held with International Heptathlon Athlete Ms. Nandini Agasara. Ms. Agasara shared her inspiring sporting journey with the students. She recalled that she started participating in various sports during her school days, initially driven by an innocent competitive spirit. Her journey received a major boost in 2018 through the Khelo India platform, which provided her with an opportunity to pursue athletics at a higher level and represent India. She achieved several significant milestones in her sporting career. In 2022, she became an Indian Under-20 National Record Holder in the 100m hurdles and also won a Bronze Medal at the Asian Championship. At the Asian Athletics Championships 2025, she made the country proud by winning a historic Gold Medal. Ms. Agasara credited initiatives such as Khelo India for providing young athletes with opportunities to identify, nurture and develop their sporting talent. She also acknowledged the holistic support extended by the Government of India to Indian athletes during international competitions.
The Khelo India Dialogue also provided a platform for the youth of IIT Bombay to share their ideas, suggestions and perspectives on further strengthening the sports ecosystem in India. Students shared suggestions relating to sports infrastructure, opportunities for young athletes, grassroots participation, access to sporting facilities and creating a stronger culture of sports among students and youth. Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri Ramdas Athawale and Director, IIT Bombay, Prof. Shireesh Kedare, subsequently addressed the gathering and provided guidance on promoting and developing the sports ecosystem at IIT Bombay and encouraging greater participation of students in sports and physical activities.
As part of the programme, a Nasha-Mukta Pledge was administered to the students and youth. The participants pledged to stay away from drugs and substance abuse and contribute towards building a healthy, strong and drug-free India. The programme was organised by IIT Bombay in coordination with My Bharat Mumbai, under the coordination of Deputy Director, My Bharat Mumbai, Shri Anup Ingole. The Khelo India Dialogue at IIT Bombay served as an important platform for connecting Mumbai’s youth with the Prime Minister’s vision for a stronger sporting ecosystem, greater youth participation in sports and a healthier and more vibrant India.
***
Edgar Coelho/Parshuram Kor

title: Nuclear Energy Technology in India
indiaConnection: This release is an official Government of India public record.

sources.title: Nuclear Energy Technology in India
sources.evidenceText:
India's nuclear programme is guided by a strategy of technological self-reliance, developed to overcome historical fuel embargoes while harnessing the country's vast thorium reserves. At its core is the indigenously designed three-stage nuclear power programme, which enables a gradual transition from uranium- to thorium-based fuel cycles. By advancing indigenous innovation, expanding clean and reliable electricity generation, and ensuring long-term energy security, the programme is contributing to India's vision of sustainable development and achieving 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047.
Nuclear Energy Supporting India's Sustainable Energy Security
India is committed to building a secure, sustainable, and self-reliant energy future to support its journey towards Viksit Bharat . Recognising the growing demand for clean, reliable and stable baseload electricity, the Government of India has placed nuclear energy at the core of its long-term energy strategy. Nuclear power provides round-the-clock, low-carbon electricity, complementing renewable energy while ensuring grid stability. It also reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and supports India's climate commitments. Guided by the vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat , the Government of India is developing robust indigenous capabilities across the entire nuclear fuel cycle, including reactor design, fuel fabrication, waste management, and advanced technologies.
India currently operates 24 nuclear power reactors with a total installed capacity of 8.78 GW . Nine reactor units , with a combined capacity of 7.5 GW , are under construction. The Government has also approved 10 indigenous Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) in fleet mode and pre-project activities for two 500 MW Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) . Recent policy initiatives, including the Nuclear Energy Mission (2025–26) and the SHANTI Act, 2025 , are accelerating capacity expansion, strengthening domestic manufacturing, promoting innovation and enabling greater private sector participation. Together, these initiatives are creating a resilient nuclear ecosystem that supports sustainable development and advances India's goal of achieving 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047 .
Baseload Electricity
Stable baseload electricity is the minimum, uninterrupted amount of power an electric grid needs to remain operational. It acts as the backbone of our power supply, ensuring reliable electricity for hospitals, communication networks, defence establishments, industries, and other essential services. Reliable baseload power is essential for economic growth, national security, and disaster resilience.
Understanding Nuclear Energy: An Overview
Nuclear power plants generate electricity by harnessing heat released through a carefully controlled process called nuclear fission. The heat converts water into steam, which drives a turbine connected to a generator. The generated electricity powers homes, industries, and essential services. The entire process operates within multiple engineered safety barriers and a robust regulatory framework.
Nuclear Fuel
Nuclear fuel is the material placed inside a nuclear reactor to generate electricity. Its atoms split through nuclear fission and release large amounts of heat. The heat converts water into steam. The steam drives turbines to generate electricity.
Nuclear reactor fuels can be fissile, which directly sustain the chain reaction or fertile , which are first converted into fissile fuels inside the reactor. The most common nuclear fuels are Natural Uranium , Uranium-235 (U-235) , Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU) , Plutonium-239 (Pu-239) , and Mixed Oxide (MOX) fuel .
Most countries, including the United States, France, China, Japan, South Korea, Canada, and Russia, use Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU) in Light Water Reactors. India mainly uses Natural Uranium in Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) , which do not require uranium enrichment. India also uses MOX fuel in its Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) .
India's uranium reserves are of low grade and therefore need to be supplemented through imports. India, however, has abundant reserves of thorium (Th-232). This is a fertile rather than fissile radioactive material, found mainly in the coastal sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand . Inside a reactor, Th-232 absorbs a neutron and transforms into Uranium-233 , which is fissile. India's long-term nuclear strategy is centred on utilising its abundant thorium reserves , through its three-stage nuclear power programme.
India's Three-Stage Nuclear Programme
Dr. Homi J. Bhabha proposed the three-stage nuclear power programme in 1954 to maximise the use of India's indigenous resources and achieve long-term energy security. India achieved a major milestone in April 2026 when the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam attained first criticality . A breeder reactor is one that produces more fissile material or fuel while generating electricity. This marked the beginning of the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear power programme. The milestone brings India closer to harnessing its abundant thorium resources for long-term, clean, and self-reliant energy security. To read further: A New Chapter in India's Nuclear Journey
In the first stage , Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) use natural uranium to generate electricity. The spent fuel is reprocessed to recover plutonium, which becomes the primary input for the second stage. In the second stage , Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) use this plutonium to generate electricity while breeding additional fissile material. They also produce uranium-233 from thorium, laying the groundwork for the third stage. In the third stage , thorium-based reactors use uranium-233 to harness India's abundant thorium reserves. Each stage feeds into the next, unlocking long-term energy security.
The Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) led the design, development, testing, safety assessment, commissioning and indigenisation of India's Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) . Through close collaboration with Indian industry, IGCAR achieved nearly 90 per cent domestic manufacturing of the reactor's equipment and systems, strengthening India's self-reliance in advanced nuclear technology and supporting the country's second stage of the Three Stage Nuclear Power Programme.
Nuclear Reaction
A nuclear reaction releases energy from the nucleus of an atom. The two main types are nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Nuclear power plants use nuclear fission.
In a nuclear reactor, a neutron strikes the nucleus of a uranium or plutonium atom, causing it to split into two smaller atoms. This process, known as nuclear fission, releases a large amount of heat and additional neutrons. These neutrons trigger further fission reactions, creating a carefully controlled chain reaction. The heat generated is used to convert water into high-pressure steam. The steam drives a turbine, which is connected to a generator. As the turbine rotates, the generator produces electricity.
Nuclear Fusion
Nuclear fusion combines two light atoms to form a heavier atom. Fusion powers the Sun and stars. It can produce much more energy than fission. However, fusion technology is still under development for commercial electricity generation.
Nuclear Reactors
The nuclear reactor is the heart of a nuclear power plant, where the process of nuclear fission is safely controlled to generate heat. It contains nuclear fuel, such as uranium or plutonium, control rods to regulate the fission reaction, a coolant to transfer the heat produced, and multiple safety systems to ensure safe and reliable operation.
India primarily uses Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) , which operate on natural uranium. The country also operates Boiling Water Reactors (BWRs) and Pressurised Water Reactors (PWRs) . India is advancing Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) to utilise plutonium and support the transition to thorium-based reactors. India is also developing Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) as the next generation of nuclear technology.
Small Modular Reactor
SMRs typically generate up to 300 MWe through nuclear fission. Their compact, modular design enables factory-based manufacturing, faster construction, improved quality, and phased deployment. Under the Nuclear Energy Mission , announced in the Union Budget 2025–26 , the Government has allocated ₹ 20,000 crore for the research, design, development, and deployment of indigenous SMRs. India is developing the 220 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200) , jointly designed by BARC and NPCIL , the 55 MWe SMR-55 , and a High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactor for hydrogen production. The Government aims to operationalise at least five indigenous SMRs by 2033 .
Classification of Nuclear Reactors
Nuclear reactors are designed for different applications. Large conventional reactors (700–1,600 MW) supply continuous baseload power to national grids, cities, and industries. Small Modular Reactors (up to 300 MW) and Micro Reactors (up to 20 MW) serve remote areas, replace retiring coal plants, supply industrial process heat, and support hydrogen production.
Nuclear Waste
Nuclear waste is the radioactive material generated during the operation of a nuclear power plant. It includes used nuclear fuel and other materials, such as protective clothing, filters, tools, and equipment, that become radioactive after being used in the plant. Since it emits radiation, it is managed under strict safety standards to ensure the protection of people and the environment.
India follows a closed nuclear fuel cycle, where spent nuclear fuel is reprocessed to recover valuable materials for reuse in future reactors. The remaining high-level radioactive waste is immobilised and safely stored, reducing waste and supporting India's three-stage nuclear power programme.
Vitrification Technology
India is among the few countries with vitrification technology for high-level radioactive waste. The process converts high-level radioactive waste into a stable glass form, making it safer for long-term storage, transport, and eventual disposal.
Powering India's Clean Energy Future
India's nuclear energy programme reflects the country's commitment to innovation, sustainability and self-reliance. By combining advanced technologies with rigorous safety standards and indigenous capabilities, nuclear energy is helping build a secure and resilient energy future. As the nation progresses towards Viksit Bharat, nuclear energy will continue to complement other clean energy sources, supporting economic growth, environmental sustainability and long-term energy security.
